ChIP-seq analysis

The description of the practical is adapted from Chapter 9 of Altuna Akalin’s book: Computational Genomics with R

Description of the practical

In this practical, we will use the RStudio Server available here: https://rstudio.dlab.elte.hu/. Please log in using the same username and password as you use with ssh login to the server.

This practical is an adaptation of Chapter 9 of Akalin’s book. The original chapter uses GM12878 datasets distributed with the compGenomRData package, and, for computational reasons, works on human chromosome 21. We will follow the same logic, but adapt the analysis to real ENCODE histone ChIP-seq experiments in human K562 cells (ENCODE Project Consortium 2012; Davis 2018), focusing on:

  • H3K27ac: ENCSR000AKP
  • H3K4me1: ENCSR000AKS
  • shared Input control: ENCSR000AKY

An Input control is a DNA sample that has not been enriched by the antibody, so it provides a picture of the background signal caused by random fragmentation, sequencing coverage, and mapping biases. You can think of it as the “background noise” or baseline of the experiment: it helps us decide whether a ChIP signal is a true enrichment peak or just part of the general genomic landscape.

Because in session 3 (Genomics, Part 1, with Orsolya Pipek) we already covered the transformation of FASTQ files into analysis-ready BAM files, and in session 7 (Transcriptomics, Part 1, with Eszter Ari) we revisited read quality filtering, mapping, and read counting for RNA-seq, this lab will start from released aligned and processed ENCODE files. The point here is not to repeat generic alignment practice, but to focus on the ChIP-specific questions of enrichment quality, peak calling, and regulatory interpretation.

We will also add one guided downstream extension inspired by the later part of Chapter 9: using ChromHMM to binarise the K562 histone ChIP-seq data on chr21, learn a small chromatin-state model, and interpret peak-derived regulatory candidates in the context of the learned states.

ImportantWhy this matters

ChromHMM is an algorithm that converts data from chromatin signal into simple presence/absence patterns (binary, just 0 or 1) across genomic bins, using a hidden Markov model to group recurring combinations of marks into interpretable chromatin states. This will help us move one step further and ask what kind of regulatory element a region may represent (for example, active enhancers, active promoters, or just inactive chromatin).

After this lab, you will be able to:

  • organise ChIP-seq metadata into a reproducible sample sheet
  • compare histone ChIP samples and Input controls using genome-wide binned signals
  • inspect ChIP-seq signal tracks in a genome browser
  • evaluate enrichment quality using strand cross-correlation and GC-bias plots
  • compare read distributions across functional genomic regions
  • call broad histone peaks on a chromosome subset
  • evaluate peak quality using reads-in-peaks summaries
  • intersect H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peaks to define candidate active regulatory regions
  • annotate candidate enhancer-like regions to nearby genes
  • generate ChromHMM binarised files, learn a small chromatin-state model, and interpret peak-derived candidate regulatory regions in the context of the learned states

As usual, the questions will be denoted as follows:

NoteT0 Q0

Questions to solve go here.

The dataset we will work with

The experimental setup, together with released files and metadata, can be found on the ENCODE portal (Davis 2018):

  • ENCSR000AKP: H3K27ac ChIP-seq on human K562
  • ENCSR000AKS: H3K4me1 ChIP-seq on human K562
  • ENCSR000AKY: Input control ChIP-seq on human K562

The experiments are released public datasets, which means that they are not toy examples or simulated data. Public ENCODE K562 ChIP-seq data have been reused in real biological studies to support the interpretation of regulatory regions (ENCODE Project Consortium 2012; Barbarani 2017). This is one of the main strengths of functional genomics: once high-quality data are released, they can be re-analysed to ask new questions.

ImportantTake into account

Although GM12878 is a canonical ENCODE cell line and very useful for teaching, this practical uses datasets from K562 (also from ENCODE) so that you work directly with public research data that can be linked to a published biological application. In particular, the selected K562 datasets were used to interpret candidate regulatory regions in a peer-reviewed study on SOX6 regulation in K562 cells https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-14336-6 (Barbarani 2017).

To keep the practical feasible in a 3-hour workshop, we will mimic the strategy used in Chapter 9 and work on chromosome 21 only. We will therefore download the selected ENCODE files and create smaller chr21-restricted BAM files for the downstream steps. If that becomes too cumbersome during the practical, a prepared backup of the chr21-restricted BAM files and the selected bigWig files will also be available.1

A typical working directory might contain the following files:

directory contents
0000_metadata/ manifest template, experiment notes, chromosome sizes
0001_bam/ downloaded ENCODE BAM files, locally created or copied backup chr21 BAM files, and BAI index files
0002_bigwig/ downloaded or copied signal tracks (bigWig)
0003_qc/ output folder for correlation, cross-correlation, GC, and distribution plots
0004_peaks/ MACS2 peak calling results
0005_annotation/ gene annotation objects and exported genomic category BED files generated in Task 6
0006_results/ overlap tables, FRiP-style summaries, annotated regulatory regions
0007_states/ ChromHMM input tables, binarised files, learned models, state labels, and state-overlap summaries

Task 0: Setting up the RStudio working environment for the ChIP-seq practical

  1. Go to the RStudio Server in a browser on your computer: https://rstudio.dlab.elte.hu/
  2. Create a New Project: File ➔ New Project … in a New directory ➔ where Project Type is New Project with Directory name: 09_ChIPseq
  3. Create a new R Script file: File ➔ New File ➔ R Script, save it (give it a name). Here you can type, evaluate (by Ctrl+Enter), and save the commands.
  4. Create a new Shell Script file: File ➔ New File ➔ Shell Script, save it (give it a name). Here you can type, evaluate (by Ctrl+Enter), and save the commands.
  5. In the Terminal tab of your RStudio project, create the folder structure for the practical. Because you are working inside the 09_ChIPseq project, these folders will be created inside that project directory.
mkdir -p 0000_metadata 0001_bam 0002_bigwig 0003_qc 0004_peaks 0005_annotation 0006_results 0007_states 0007_states/binary 0007_states/model

In Task 1, you will either download the selected BAM and bigWig files yourself from the ENCODE portal using wget, or, if needed, copy the prepared backup files from the shared course folder. For now, only link the chromosome-size file needed later in the practical. The genomic annotation files for 0005_annotation/ will be generated locally in Task 6 from Bioconductor.

ln -s /shared/OMICS/practical_09/chrom_sizes/hg38_chr21.chrom.sizes 0000_metadata/

Save the script files after typing code frequently. Keeping a clean shell history and reproducible file structure is part of the analysis itself! It is useful to separate R code from shell commands when a practical mixes command-line tools and Bioconductor workflows (as it was in session 7).

Before starting the analysis, check that Java and ChromHMM are available:

java -version
java -jar /shared/software/ChromHMM-1.27/ChromHMM/ChromHMM.jar LearnModel

If the second command prints the LearnModel usage message, the ChromHMM installation is working.

Introduction to ChIP-seq data analysis

What is ChIP-seq?

ChIP-seq (chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing) is used to identify genomic regions associated with a protein of interest. In the context of histone ChIP-seq, the immunoprecipitation enriches for DNA fragments carrying a specific histone modification, and the mapped reads provide a genome-wide profile of where that mark is enriched. In addition, it is a very important technique to discover the state and function of chromatin regions outside the limits of genes and exons.

ImportantTake into account

Although this practical focuses on histone modifications, ChIP-seq is not limited to histone marks. It is also widely used to profile sequence-specific transcription factors (which can test direct gene regulation by proteins) and other chromatin-associated proteins or protein complexes, provided that a suitable antibody and experimental design are available (Park 2009; Landt 2012).

Chapter 9 of Akalin’s book emphasises that ChIP-seq analysis has at least three logically distinct parts:

  1. understanding which factors affect data quality,
  2. evaluating whether the immunoprecipitation enrichment was successful,
  3. identifying and interpreting enriched genomic regions.

In practice, this means that quality control is not finished once the reads are mapped. For ChIP-seq, we also need to check whether the biological enrichment makes sense.

Why these two histone marks?

We will analyse two histone modifications that are often associated with regulatory DNA:

  • H3K4me1 is frequently associated with enhancer-like regions, especially distal regulatory elements (Heintzman 2009).
  • H3K27ac is frequently associated with active regulatory elements (such as enhancers or promoters) and can, for example, distinguish active enhancers from poised enhancer-like regions (Creyghton 2010).

By combining them, we can answer the more biological question “which regions look like active enhancer-like loci?”

This also makes the final interpretation step richer: simple peak overlap suggests candidate active regulatory loci, while chromatin-state labels help us ask whether those same loci are better explained as enhancer-like, promoter-like, or other functional states.

These two histone marks have been selected to provide an introduction to epigenomics data analysis. Larger reference-mapping projects often profile broader histone panels (for example, promoter-associated H3K4me3, transcribed-region H3K36me3, Polycomb-associated H3K27me3, and heterochromatin-associated H3K9me3) because they enable much richer chromatin-state interpretation than is possible with only two marks. In the Roadmap Epigenomics analysis, for example, 111 reference epigenomes were organised around a core set of five histone modifications, with additional marks available in more deeply profiled samples (Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium 2015).

What are we going to do in this practical?

We have adapted the workflow from Akalin’s book to K562 histone ChIP-seq, and we focus on the parts of Chapter 9 that are most informative for a histone-mark workshop:

  • ChIP quality control
  • broad peak calling
  • peak quality control
  • peak annotation
  • integration of two enhancer-associated histone marks
  • interpretation of peak-derived regions in the context of chromatin states

The first eight tasks follow the main logic of Akalin’s book (Chapter 9): quality control first, then peak calling, then peak-level interpretation. Two final tasks extend that logic further. Task 9, Stateforge, asks whether the peak-derived regions are supported by a small chromatin-state model. Task 10, Karyoscape, then turns that result into a chromosome-level visualisation of candidate regulatory regions and learned chromatin states along chr21.

Factors that affect ChIP-seq experiment and analysis quality

The quality of a ChIP-seq experiment depends on more than sequencing itself. Important factors include (Landt 2012):

  • antibody specificity: does the antibody truly enrich the target mark?
  • sequencing depth: do we have enough reads to detect enrichment?
  • PCR duplication: are we over-counting technical duplicates?
  • biological replicates: do replicates agree with one another?
  • control experiments: is an Input sample available for background comparison?

In today’s practical, we will not experimentally validate the antibody, but we will still use the consequences of these factors as interpretation criteria for the data.

ChIP quality control

There are four central steps of ChIP quality control:

  1. sample correlation clustering,
  2. data visualisation in a genome browser,
  3. plus/minus strand cross-correlation,
  4. GC-bias visualisation.

We will add one more useful diagnostic for histone ChIP-seq: the genomic distribution of reads or windows.

Task 1: Metaforge - reading the experimental setup and building the sample sheet

The first step is to turn the information on the ENCODE pages into a reproducible manifest. Because the ENCODE portal may show multiple released files for the same replicate, use the exact selection rules below so that everyone creates the same manifest file.

  1. Visit the three ENCODE experiment pages:

    • ENCSR000AKP: H3K27ac ChIP-seq on human K562
    • ENCSR000AKS: H3K4me1 ChIP-seq on human K562
    • ENCSR000AKY: Input control ChIP-seq on human K562

  2. For each experiment, open the File details tab, set the genome build to GRCh38, and leave Include deprecated files unchecked.

  3. Use only the following released GRCh38 processed-data section for each experiment:

    • ENCSR000AKP → ENCODE4 v1.8.0 GRCh38 (ENCAN866TOS)
    • ENCSR000AKS → ENCODE4 v1.8.0 GRCh38 (ENCAN211AVB)
    • ENCSR000AKY → ENCODE4 v1.5.1 GRCh38 (ENCAN410JBG)

  4. From the selected section, record:

    • one released BAM,
    • and, for the histone-mark samples, one released signal bigWig.

  5. For the BAM, choose the file for biological replicate 1 and technical replicate 1_1.

  6. If more than one released BAM is available for the same biological and technical replicate, choose the file whose Output field is exactly alignments.2 Do not use files labelled unfiltered alignments.

  7. For the bigWig, use a released signal track from the same selected GRCh38 processed-data section. For the histone-mark samples (H3K27ac_r1 and H3K4me1_r1), choose the file whose Output field is exactly fold change over control.3 Do not use signal p-value bigWigs. For the input sample (Input_r1), leave the bigwig field empty, because in this practical the input will be inspected from its BAM file rather than from a separate bigWig track.

  8. Do not use:

    • hg19 files,
    • archived analyses,
    • unfiltered alignments,
    • signal p-value bigWigs for the histone-mark samples,
    • or released peak files.

  9. Save the result as a tab-separated text file called 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv.

In this manifest, the column replicate refers to the biological replicate number. In this task, use biological replicate 1 for all three samples. Technical replicate information is used only to select the correct files on the ENCODE portal; when a technical replicate is shown, use technical replicate 1_1. The manifest does not include a BAI column; index files will be created locally from the selected BAM files before they are used downstream. In the bam column, record the original downloaded ENCODE BAM filename, because that is the filename used by the wget commands above. If you use the backup route instead, Task 2 will look for the prepared local files named H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam, H3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam, and Input_r1.chr21.bam.

A minimal manifest should contain at least the following columns:

sample_id experiment assembly analysis mark replicate role control bam bigwig
H3K27ac_r1 ENCSR000AKP GRCh38 ENCAN866TOS H3K27ac 1 ChIP ENCSR000AKY file.bam file.bigWig
H3K4me1_r1 ENCSR000AKS GRCh38 ENCAN211AVB H3K4me1 1 ChIP ENCSR000AKY file.bam file.bigWig
Input_r1 ENCSR000AKY GRCh38 ENCAN410JBG Input 1 Input NA file.bam “”

The downstream analyses in this task use the local chr21-restricted BAM files prepared in Task 1. If you followed the download route, those files were created from the original ENCODE BAM files with samtools. If you used the backup route, they were copied from the shared course folder. In both cases, the files used below should be H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam, H3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam, and Input_r1.chr21.bam.

manifest <- data.frame(
  sample_id  = c("H3K27ac_r1", "H3K4me1_r1", "Input_r1"),
  experiment = c("ENCSR000AKP", "ENCSR000AKS", "ENCSR000AKY"),
  assembly   = c("GRCh38", "GRCh38", "GRCh38"),
  analysis   = c("ENCAN866TOS", "ENCAN211AVB", "ENCAN410JBG"),
  mark       = c("H3K27ac", "H3K4me1", "Input"),
  replicate  = c(1, 1, 1),
  role       = c("ChIP", "ChIP", "Input"),
  control    = c("ENCSR000AKY", "ENCSR000AKY", "NA"),
  bam        = c("file.bam", "file.bam", "file.bam"),
  bigwig     = c("file.bigWig", "file.bigWig", ""),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

write.table(
  manifest,
  file = "0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv",
  sep = "\t",
  quote = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

You can then read the file back into R to check that it was written correctly:

manifest <- read.delim("0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
manifest
  1. After saving the manifest, use it to download the selected ENCODE files directly into your project folders with wget. The bam and bigwig columns store the ENCODE filenames needed for the direct download links.
# download the three BAM files listed in the manifest
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | cut -f9 | while read f; do
  acc="${f%%.*}"
  wget -nc -P 0001_bam "https://www.encodeproject.org/files/${acc}/@@download/${f}"
done
# create chr21-restricted BAM files and index them
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | \
while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample_id experiment assembly analysis mark replicate role control bam bigwig; do
  in="0001_bam/${bam}"
  out="0001_bam/${sample_id}.chr21.bam"

  samtools index "${in}"
  samtools view -b -o "${out}" "${in}" chr21
  samtools index "${out}"
done
# optional: remove the original full-genome BAM files after checking that the chr21 files were created correctly
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | cut -f9 | while read f; do
  rm -f "0001_bam/${f}" "0001_bam/${f}.bai" "0001_bam/${f%.bam}.bai"
done
# download the two histone bigWig files listed in the manifest
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | cut -f10 | grep -v '^$' | while read f; do
  acc="${f%%.*}"
  wget -nc -P 0002_bigwig "https://www.encodeproject.org/files/${acc}/@@download/${f}"
done

  1. If downloading and subsetting the original BAM files becomes too slow or cumbersome during the practical, a prepared backup route is available.4

  2. Keep the original downloaded ENCODE BAM filenames in the manifest, because they are used by the download command above. The downstream analyses in this practical will use the local chr21-restricted files called H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam, H3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam, and Input_r1.chr21.bam.

Task 2: Tilerhythm - clustering samples using 1-kb genomic windows

In Chapter 9, sample clustering is performed by counting reads in 1-kb tiling windows, normalising the counts, and comparing the resulting signal profiles. This is a quick way to see whether:

  • replicates are concordant,
  • ChIP samples separate from Input,
  • marks with related genomic behaviour resemble one another.

We will do the same on chr21.

The downstream analyses in this task use the local chr21-restricted BAM files prepared in Task 1. If you followed the download route, those files were created from the original ENCODE BAM files with samtools. If you used the backup route, they were copied from the shared course folder. In both cases, the files used below should be H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam, H3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam, and Input_r1.chr21.bam.

The main output of this task should be a correlation heatmap saved as 0003_qc/Task2_tile_correlation_heatmap_1kb.png. Treat this figure as a first exploratory summary of the data on chr21: it can already reveal whether the samples follow a biologically sensible overall pattern, but it is not yet a full quality-control assessment.

This also connects with the session last week (session 8, Transcriptomics, Part 2, with Eszter Ari): there, clustering and PCA were used to compare samples on the basis of gene-expression matrices; here, the same exploratory logic is reused, but the rows are now genomic bins, or windows, rather than genes, and the signal reflects chromatin occupancy rather than transcript abundance.

First, load the libraries that are going to be used:

library(GenomicRanges)
library(GenomicAlignments)
library(pheatmap)

Read the manifest

manifest <- read.delim("0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

Define chromosome 21 tiling windows for GRCh38

chr21_length <- 46709983
bins <- tileGenome(
  seqlengths = c(chr21 = chr21_length),
  tilewidth = 1000,
  cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE
)

Local chr21 BAM files used downstream

bam_files <- file.path("0001_bam", paste0(manifest$sample_id, ".chr21.bam"))
names(bam_files) <- manifest$sample_id

Check that all chr21 BAM files are present

stopifnot(all(file.exists(bam_files)))

Check that all chr21 BAM files are indexed

bam_has_index <- file.exists(paste0(bam_files, ".bai")) |
  file.exists(sub("\\.bam$", ".bai", bam_files))
stopifnot(all(bam_has_index))

Since we know that the files are single-end, we will use singleEnd = TRUE, but in other projects the BAM files can be paired-end, and therefore we would need to set singleEnd = FALSE and fragments = TRUE.

se <- summarizeOverlaps(
  features = bins,
  reads = bam_files,
  mode = "Union",
  singleEnd = TRUE,
  ignore.strand = TRUE
)

counts <- assay(se)
cpm <- t(t(counts) / colSums(counts) * 1e6)
cor_mat <- cor(log10(cpm + 1), method = "spearman")

png("0003_qc/Task2_tile_correlation_heatmap_1kb.png", width = 1200, height = 900, res = 150)
pheatmap(
  cor_mat,
  main = "ChIP-seq sample correlations on chr21 (1 kb)",
  fontsize = 11,
  border_color = NA
)
dev.off()

The heatmap below shows the pairwise similarity between the three samples across 1-kb windows on chr21.

A few general points are worth keeping in mind when looking at this figure. The diagonal is always equal to 1, because each sample is perfectly correlated with itself, while the off-diagonal cells summarise the similarity between different samples across all windows. Here we are using a simple exploratory approach: counts are summarised in 1-kb bins, scaled to counts per million, log-transformed, and compared with Spearman correlation. This already gives a useful first impression of how similar the samples are, but it is still a lightweight summary rather than a full ChIP-seq quality-control analysis. The main goal is therefore to look for broad, biologically sensible patterns rather than to over-interpret small differences in colour or branch length. Because this analysis is restricted to chr21, includes only three samples, and does not use replicate averaging, the heatmap is best treated as an initial orientation step rather than a definitive biological result.

If we increase the bin size from 1 kb to 10 kb, we average the signal over larger genomic regions. This reduces local variation and tends to increase the apparent similarity between samples. The heatmap therefore becomes smoother and the correlations become higher, but we lose some fine-scale resolution.

NoteT2 Q1

Do the two histone marks cluster more closely with each other or with the Input sample?

NoteT2 Q2

NoteT2 Q3

Task 2 conclusion

At this stage, the correlation heatmap should be viewed as a first exploratory sanity check. Even with a simple workflow based on chr21 only, the result is already informative: if the two histone-mark samples appear more similar to each other than to the Input sample, that is a reassuring sign that the ChIP-seq profiles contain structured biological signal beyond the background represented by the control.

At the same time, this is still a limited analysis. We have not yet carried out a full ChIP-seq quality-control workflow, and the result should therefore be interpreted with caution. In this task, the heatmap is useful mainly because it helps us check whether the data show a plausible overall pattern before moving on to more focused downstream analyses.

Task 3: Trackorama - visualisation in a genome browser

It’s a good idea doing a direct visual inspection of the signal in a genome browser. Even when the statistics look acceptable, the browser can reveal:

  • unexpected background,
  • broad versus focal enrichment,
  • suspicious local artefacts,
  • agreement or disagreement between ChIP and Input.

IGV should already be familiar from session 2, when Eszter Ari introduced it in the context of next-generation sequencing, and from session 7, where it was used to inspect mapped RNA-seq reads. What we are going to change here is the interpretation: instead of looking for exon-aware alignment patterns, we will be looking for enrichment profiles above Input background.

For this exercise, use IGV or an equivalent browser and inspect:

  • a known chr21 gene locus such as RUNX1, and
  • one additional region chosen by the teacher or by you.

Load:

  1. the GRCh38 gene annotation,
  2. the H3K27ac signal track,
  3. the H3K4me1 signal track,
  4. the Input BAM track.

For this practical, use bigWig files for the two histone marks and the chr21 BAM file for the input sample. The input bigWig field is intentionally left empty in the manifest so that everyone uses the same browser setup, whether they followed the download route or the backup-copy route.

# Example only: open IGV from a normal terminal if available
igv.sh &

Alternatively, you may visualise selected loci using Gviz in R.

library(Gviz)

h3k27ac_bw <- file.path("0002_bigwig", manifest$bigwig[manifest$sample_id == "H3K27ac_r1"])
h3k4me1_bw <- file.path("0002_bigwig", manifest$bigwig[manifest$sample_id == "H3K4me1_r1"])
input_bam  <- file.path("0001_bam", "Input_r1.chr21.bam")

axisTrack <- GenomeAxisTrack()

h3k27acTrack <- DataTrack(
  range = h3k27ac_bw,
  chromosome = "chr21",
  genome = "hg38",
  name = "H3K27ac",
  type = "histogram"
)

h3k4me1Track <- DataTrack(
  range = h3k4me1_bw,
  chromosome = "chr21",
  genome = "hg38",
  name = "H3K4me1",
  type = "histogram"
)

inputTrack <- AlignmentsTrack(
  range = input_bam,
  chromosome = "chr21",
  genome = "hg38",
  isPaired = FALSE,
  name = "Input"
)

plotTracks(
  list(axisTrack, h3k27acTrack, h3k4me1Track, inputTrack),
  chromosome = "chr21",
  from = 37000000,
  to = 37200000,
  sizes = c(0.6, 1.5, 1.5, 1.8)
)

png("0003_qc/Task3_Gviz_tracks_RUNX1.png", width = 1200, height = 900, res = 150)
plotTracks(
  list(axisTrack, h3k27acTrack, h3k4me1Track, inputTrack),
  chromosome = "chr21",
  from = 37000000,
  to = 37200000,
  sizes = c(0.6, 1.5, 1.5, 1.8)
)
dev.off()

For this task, we will focus on the gene RUNX1, because it is a transcription factor that regulates the differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells into mature blood cells. As a biologically relevant hematopoietic regulator on chr21, it is a sensible locus to inspect in K562 cells. This is also a useful adaptation of the original paper: there, the main genome-browser style example is the SAR1B–SEC24A locus on chr5, but in this practical we restrict ourselves to chr21, so RUNX1 provides a good chromosome-21 alternative.

Look for the coordinates of RUNX1 (for example on ensembl.org), and replace the from/to parameters in the code, to plot a region of 30 kb around the promoter (take into account the direction of the gene). 5

You should get something like this:

In this example, the two histone-mark tracks are shown together with the Input BAM track over a small promoter-centred region near RUNX1 on chr21. The main point is not to measure exact signal values by eye, but to compare the overall shape of the profiles and to ask whether the ChIP signals rise above the background seen in the Input track. The Input track will often look rougher and less smooth than the bigWig tracks, because it is drawn directly from aligned reads rather than from a processed signal summary. As in the previous tasks, this is best treated as a qualitative browser view that helps interpretation, not as a formal statistical result.

Task 4: Strandscape - plus/minus strand cross-correlation

In session 3 (Genomics, Part 1), quality control mostly meant checking sequence-level or alignment-level properties. Here we move one level further: even if a file is already mapped and technically usable, we still need to ask whether the immunoprecipitation created a meaningful enrichment pattern, which is a specifically ChIP-seq way of thinking about QC.

A key common diagnostic is plus/minus strand cross-correlation. The idea is that a successful ChIP experiment should enrich DNA fragments of a characteristic length. If the reads on the plus and minus strands are shifted relative to one another by the fragment size, their cross-correlation profile should show a peak near that distance.

In ChIP-seq strand cross-correlation, the peaks are observed in a cross-correlation profile, not at specific genomic coordinates. The x-axis represents the strand shift (in base pairs), and the y-axis represents the cross-correlation value obtained after shifting the plus- and minus-strand coverage tracks relative to each other. Two peaks are often observed: one near the read length (the so-called phantom peak) and one near the fragment length. The phantom peak is a known short-read mappability artefact, whereas the fragment-length peak reflects the clustering of sequenced fragments around enriched regions. In a good enriched dataset, the fragment-length peak should be higher than the phantom peak, meaning that the cross-correlation value at the fragment-length shift is stronger than the read-length artefact (Landt et al. 2012; ENCODE Data Coordination Center 2020). By contrast, if the phantom peak is as high as or higher than the fragment-length peak, the signal is dominated by the read-length artefact rather than by the expected enrichment pattern, which is a warning sign of weak ChIP enrichment (and therefore, a low signal-to-noise ratio). A practical way to think about the two peaks is this: the phantom peak is expected near the left-hand side of the plot, at a small shift close to the read length, while the fragment-length peak is expected further to the right, at a larger shift corresponding to the average DNA fragment size.

The two diagrams below (Landt 2012) illustrate the idea. The first one shows the typical shapes of successful, marginal, and failed cross-correlation profiles, while the second highlights the expected positions of the phantom peak and the ChIP/fragment-length peak.

Taken together, these figures show why the fragment-length peak should dominate in a good ChIP-seq experiment: it reflects the expected clustering of reads around enriched fragments, whereas the phantom peak is a short-read artefact. If the phantom peak is higher, the profile looks more like a marginal or failed experiment than a successful one (Landt et al. 2012).

The NSC and RSC (Normalised and Relative Strand cross-correlation coefficients) are summary scores that compare the strength of the fragment-length peak with background and with the read-length phantom peak. They matter here because they help us judge whether the sample shows genuine ChIP enrichment rather than mostly technical artefact.

This is often calculated with spp or phantompeakqualtools, and it is one of the ENCODE-style ChIP quality diagnostics emphasised in the guidelines literature (Landt 2012). In this practical, we will use the shared run_spp.R script located at /shared/software/phantompeakqualtools/run_spp.R.

We can run it on the terminal from the folder where it has been downloaded for this course, asnd using the data for the H3K27ac:

Rscript /shared/software/phantompeakqualtools/run_spp.R \
  -c="~/09_ChIPseq/0001_bam/H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam" \
  -odir="~/09_ChIPseq/0003_qc" \
  -savp="~/09_ChIPseq/0003_qc/Task4_H3K27ac_r1_crosscorr.pdf" \
  -out="~/09_ChIPseq/0003_qc/Task4_H3K27ac_r1_crosscorr.tsv"

Repeat the procedure for H3K4me1 and Input. Then compare the console messages and the resulting PDF plots across the three samples.

If the shared installation under /shared/software/phantompeakqualtools is not available on your system, use the provided output files and the annotated example below for interpretation, then continue with the questions.

A typical successful run produces console output like the following:

How to read this output:

  • The first block mainly confirms which input file was used and where the results were written. This is useful to check that the script is analysing the correct BAM file and saving the PDF and TSV files in the expected directory.
  • The line done. read 138349 fragments tells us that the program successfully read the chr21-restricted BAM file and extracted enough mapped fragments to compute a cross-correlation profile. This count is a little below what one would expect by extrapolating whole-genome depth recommendations to chr21, but it stays within the expected order of magnitude.6
  • The line ChIP data read length 36 tells us where the short-shift phantom peak is expected: in this example, around 35–40 bp.
  • The line Top 3 estimates for fragment length 170,180 is one of the most important results. It suggests that the enriched DNA fragments in this sample are roughly in that size range, which is biologically plausible for a ChIP-seq library.
  • The line Phantom peak location 40 means that the short-shift read-length artefact is strongest at a strand shift of about 40 bp. Since this dataset has a read length of 36 bp, that is where a phantom peak is expected.
  • The lines NSC and RSC are the main summary quality measures. Here, both values are higher than 1, which is encouraging, as it suggests that the signal in the sample is much higher than the background noise.
  • The final line null device 1 simply shows that the plot file was written and the graphics device was closed normally.

The cross-correlation profile captures a good fragment-length-related signal, and the summary metrics are consistent with a successful ChIP enrichment. In particular, the fragment-length signal is stronger than the short-shift phantom peak, which is the pattern we want to see. At the same time, the plot is not expected to be “beautiful” in a polished publication sense: here we are working with a chr21-restricted file, so the result should be treated as an instructive and biologically sensible QC example rather than as a full genome-wide benchmark.

Task 5: GCBloom - visualising GC bias

Sometimes datasets present technical biases due to amplification, library preparation, or sequencing chemistry. To detect them, it is often recommended in ChIP-seq analysis to plot the relationship between GC content and signal abundance (number of reads aligned) across genomic bins. One reason is that some sequencers coverage can depend on the overall GC composition of the sequenced fragment, so bins with very low or very high GC content may end up over- or under-represented even when their true biological enrichment is similar. Another reason is that PCR can amplify fragments of different base composition with unequal efficiency, which can distort coverage independently of the real ChIP signal. A common way to reduce this problem is to model the dependence of coverage on GC content and then normalise or correct the signal before downstream comparison, although this would be beyond the goals of this practical.

Here we will combine the 1-kb windows from Task 2 with the GRCh38 sequence of chr21, and we will first inspect the H3K27ac_r1 sample as a simple example before comparing it with the other two samples.

We start by loading the libraries that will be used:

library(BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38)
library(ggplot2)

We get sequences for the bins:

seqs <- getSeq(BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38, bins)

We approximate the GC fraction of each 1-kb bin:

base_counts <- letterFrequency(seqs, letters = c("G", "C"))
gc_fraction <- rowSums(base_counts) / width(seqs)

gc_df <- data.frame(
  GC = gc_fraction,
  cpm = cpm[, "H3K27ac_r1"]
)

Plotting it:

ggplot(gc_df, aes(x = GC, y = log10(cpm + 1))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  xlab("GC content in 1-kb bins") +
  ylab("log10(CPM + 1)") +
  ggtitle("H3K27ac_r1")

ggsave("0003_qc/Task5_gc_bias_H3K27ac_r1.png", width = 5, height = 4)

The figure below shows the relationship between GC content and signal abundance for the H3K27ac_r1 sample across 1-kb bins on chr21. Each point represents one genomic bin. The x-axis shows the GC fraction of the bin, that is, the proportion of bases in that 1-kb window that are either G or C. The y-axis shows log10(CPM + 1), where CPM means counts per million (the number of mapped ChIP-seq reads or fragments overlapping that 1-kb window).

Our goal is to look at the overall shape of the cloud. In particular, ask whether signal values appear roughly spread across the GC range or whether they seem to increase systematically in bins with higher GC content. This will help you decide whether a strong GC-dependent bias is obvious in this sample. If there were no GC bias, bins with different GC content would not show a systematic difference in signal abundance. In other words, the number of mapped reads per bin should not consistently increase or decrease only because the bin is more GC-rich or more AT-rich.7

Now modify the code to generate equivalent plots for H3K4me1_r1 and Input_r1. Don’t forget to update the titles, so you don’t overwrite the files.

Once you have generated all three plots, compare them side by side. A useful question is whether the two histone-mark samples show a broadly similar pattern to each other, and whether the Input sample looks different in overall spread or shape across the GC range. This will help us to decide whether one sample appears more GC-dependent than the others, which in an experiment with many samples can be of interest.

Task 6: Genomaplex - genomic distribution of reads or windows

One useful ChIP-seq quality-control view is the genomic distribution of signal across functional categories. If a ChIP sample looks too similar to the Input sample in this summary, that is a warning sign that the experiment may not show strong biological enrichment. Here we will follow the same logic, but instead of relying on pre-made BED files we will build the annotation directly in R from Bioconductor and then export the resulting BED files into 0005_annotation/ for reuse later in the practical.8

This task has four goals:

  1. create chr21 annotation categories locally from a transcript database,
  2. export those categories as BED files,
  3. assign each 1-kb bin from Task 2 to one category using a hierarchy,
  4. compare how the total ChIP signal is distributed across categories.

For H3K27ac and H3K4me1, we expect more signal in promoter-proximal or distal regulatory bins than in the Input sample (Heintzman 2009; Creyghton 2010; Landt 2012). Because genomic features can overlap, we will use a simple hierarchy:

tss > exon > intron > distal_regulatory > intergenic

Here, tss means ±1 kb around the transcription start site. For teaching purposes, we will define distal_regulatory as regions within 50 kb of a TSS but outside the tss, exon, and intron categories. This is only a working approximation of distal regulatory space, not a universal biological definition.

If you restarted RStudio since Task 2, the code below will load the libraries and recreate the bins and cpm objects automatically before doing the annotation.

library(GenomicRanges)
library(GenomicAlignments)
library(GenomicFeatures)
library(TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene)
library(rtracklayer)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

manifest <- read.delim("0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

if (!exists("bins") || !exists("cpm")) {
  chr21_length <- 46709983

  bins <- tileGenome(
    seqlengths = c(chr21 = chr21_length),
    tilewidth = 1000,
    cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE
  )

  bam_files <- file.path("0001_bam", paste0(manifest$sample_id, ".chr21.bam"))
  names(bam_files) <- manifest$sample_id

  se <- summarizeOverlaps(
    features = bins,
    reads = bam_files,
    mode = "Union",
    singleEnd = TRUE,
    ignore.strand = TRUE
  )

  counts <- assay(se)
  cpm <- t(t(counts) / colSums(counts) * 1e6)
}

chr21_length <- 46709983

Build chr21 gene, exon, intron, and promoter annotations from the TxDb database:

chr21_range  <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, chr21_length))

txdb <- TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene

genes_chr21 <- genes(txdb)
genes_chr21 <- keepSeqlevels(genes_chr21, "chr21", pruning.mode = "coarse")

exons_chr21 <- exons(txdb)
exons_chr21 <- keepSeqlevels(exons_chr21, "chr21", pruning.mode = "coarse")
exons_chr21 <- reduce(exons_chr21)

introns_chr21 <- unlist(intronsByTranscript(txdb), use.names = FALSE)
introns_chr21 <- keepSeqlevels(introns_chr21, "chr21", pruning.mode = "coarse")
introns_chr21 <- reduce(introns_chr21)

tss_chr21 <- promoters(genes_chr21, upstream = 1000, downstream = 1000)
tss_chr21 <- reduce(tss_chr21)

tss_50kb_chr21 <- promoters(genes_chr21, upstream = 50000, downstream = 50000)
tss_50kb_chr21 <- reduce(tss_50kb_chr21)

Define distal-regulatory and intergenic regions after removing promoter and gene-body overlaps:

distal_regulatory_chr21 <- GenomicRanges::setdiff(
  tss_50kb_chr21,
  reduce(c(tss_chr21, exons_chr21, introns_chr21))
)

intergenic_chr21 <- GenomicRanges::setdiff(
  chr21_range,
  reduce(c(tss_chr21, exons_chr21, introns_chr21, distal_regulatory_chr21))
)

Export annotation BED files in bedtools-compatible coordinate order, and assign each 1-kb bin to one genomic category:

dir.create("0005_annotation", showWarnings = FALSE)

export_bed_chr21 <- function(gr, file) {
  gr <- gr[order(start(gr), end(gr))]
  export(gr, file, format = "BED")
}

export_bed_chr21(genes_chr21,             "0005_annotation/chr21_genes.bed")
export_bed_chr21(tss_chr21,               "0005_annotation/chr21_tss.bed")
export_bed_chr21(exons_chr21,             "0005_annotation/chr21_exon.bed")
export_bed_chr21(introns_chr21,           "0005_annotation/chr21_intron.bed")
export_bed_chr21(distal_regulatory_chr21, "0005_annotation/chr21_distal_regulatory.bed")
export_bed_chr21(intergenic_chr21,        "0005_annotation/chr21_intergenic.bed")
export_bed_chr21(bins,                    "0005_annotation/chr21_1kb_bins.bed")

bin_category <- rep("intergenic", length(bins))
bin_category[countOverlaps(bins, distal_regulatory_chr21) > 0] <- "distal_regulatory"
bin_category[countOverlaps(bins, introns_chr21) > 0] <- "intron"
bin_category[countOverlaps(bins, exons_chr21) > 0] <- "exon"
bin_category[countOverlaps(bins, tss_chr21) > 0] <- "tss"

bin_annotation <- data.frame(
  bin_id = seq_along(bins),
  category = factor(
    bin_category,
    levels = c("tss", "exon", "intron", "distal_regulatory", "intergenic")
  )
)

Save the bin-level genomic category table for later inspection and reuse:

write.table(
  bin_annotation,
  file = "0006_results/Task6_bin_annotation_chr21.tsv",
  sep = "\t",
  quote = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

Combine CPM values with annotation and summarise signal by genomic category:

signal_df <- as.data.frame(cpm)
signal_df$bin_id <- seq_len(nrow(signal_df))

signal_long <- signal_df %>%
  left_join(bin_annotation, by = "bin_id") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(manifest$sample_id),
    names_to = "sample_id",
    values_to = "cpm"
  ) %>%
  group_by(sample_id, category) %>%
  summarise(
    total_cpm = sum(cpm),
    mean_cpm = mean(cpm),
    n_bins = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(percent_signal = 100 * total_cpm / sum(total_cpm)) %>%
  ungroup()

Write the per-sample signal summary table to the results folder:

write.table(
  signal_long,
  file = "0006_results/Task6_signal_by_category_chr21.tsv",
  sep = "\t",
  quote = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

Plot the genomic signal distribution and save the figure for interpretation:

signal_long_plot <- signal_long %>%
  mutate(
    sample_label = recode(
      sample_id,
      H3K27ac_r1 = "H3K27ac",
      H3K4me1_r1 = "H3K4me1",
      Input_r1   = "Input"
    ),
    category = factor(
      category,
      levels = c("intergenic", "distal_regulatory", "intron", "exon", "tss"),
      labels = c("Intergenic", "Distal regulatory", "Intron", "Exon", "TSS")
    )
  )

p_task6 <- ggplot(signal_long_plot, aes(x = sample_label, y = percent_signal, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 20),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Genomic category") +
  labs(
    title = "Genomic distribution of chr21 signal",
    subtitle = "Percentage of total CPM assigned to each annotation category",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "Percentage of total CPM"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

p_task6

ggsave(
  "0006_results/Task6_genomic_distribution_signal_chr21.png",
  plot = p_task6,
  width = 7.2,
  height = 4.8,
  dpi = 300
)

The first thing to check after running this code is whether the 0005_annotation/ folder now contains the exported BED files. These files were created from the Bioconductor annotation and can be reused later for bedtools or for ad hoc inspection. They are exported in coordinate order so that they can be reused directly by bedtools in later tasks without additional re-sorting.

The expected output is the figure below. It summarises how the signal from each sample is distributed across tss (Transcription Start Site), exon, intron, distal_regulatory, and intergenic bins on chr21.

This plot should be interpreted as a coarse quality-control summary rather than as a definitive biological annotation. In this dataset, H3K27ac shows the clearest relative enrichment in tss bins, whereas the Input sample has the largest relative contribution from distal_regulatory and intergenic bins. That does not mean that Input is specifically marking enhancers. A more cautious interpretation is that the Input control is not a flat background and may retain biases related to chromatin accessibility, fragmentation, and other non-specific signal; in addition, the distal_regulatory class used here is a broad proximity-based proxy rather than a validated enhancer catalogue (Park 2009; Landt 2012; Xu 2021). Relative to Input, H3K27ac still behaves more like an active regulatory mark, whereas H3K4me1 appears closer to Input in this summary, which is compatible with the broader and sometimes poised enhancer-associated nature of H3K4me1 compared with H3K27ac (Heintzman 2009; Creyghton 2010; Calo 2013).

Pay special attention to the distal_regulatory category. In this practical definition, these are non-exonic, non-intronic, non-promoter regions within 50 kb of a gene start site. They are not guaranteed to be true enhancers, and they may include a mixture of bona fide enhancers, other nearby accessible regions, and unclassified regulatory DNA. For that reason, this category is best treated as a first-pass proxy for “enhancer-like / near-regulatory space”, not as a definitive enhancer annotation.

Which genomic categories are relatively enriched in the two histone-mark samples compared with the Input sample, and which histone mark looks most different from Input?

NoteT6 Q3

Peak calling and downstream interpretation

After quality control, we will proceed to peak calling, followed by peak quality control and peak annotation. The reference book uses normR, which is very useful for teaching the logic of enrichment modelling. In this practical, however, we will use MACS2 in --broad mode (Zhang 2008)9 because:

  • it is commonly used in practice,
  • it is straightforward in a workshop setting,
  • it matches the broad nature of histone-mark enrichment reasonably well.

We will still interpret the output using the same conceptual framework as Chapter 9. In addition, after Tasks 7 and 8 we will add one final integrative step: we will use ChromHMM to binarise the two histone-mark BAM files against Input, learn a small chromatin-state model on chr21, and ask whether the peak-derived candidate regulatory regions are supported by the learned segmentation. This is not part of the chapter’s core peak-calling walkthrough, but it fits naturally with the downstream integration and genome-segmentation ideas mentioned later in Chapter 9.

There is also a nice continuity here with the genomics block: in session 3 (Genomics, Part 1), BAM files were the endpoint of raw-read processing, and in session 4 (Genomics, Part 2), samtools reappeared as part of downstream variant analysis. In today’s practical, the same kind of alignment files become the starting material for a different downstream question: not sequence variation, but chromatin enrichment and regulatory state.

Task 7: Peaksmith - peak calling and peak quality control

In this task, we turn aligned ChIP-seq reads into candidate enriched regions and then ask whether those peak sets are coherent enough to use downstream. This task has two parts:

  1. call broad peaks for each histone mark against the matched Input control,
  2. assess whether those peak sets capture a meaningful fraction of the ChIP signal and remain enriched relative to Input.

These quality-control summaries are not the final biological result of the practical. Their purpose is to decide whether the peak sets are reliable enough to carry forward into Task 8, where overlapping H3K4me1 + H3K27ac regions will be treated as candidate active regulatory loci, into Task 9, where a simple ChromHMM segmentation will test whether that interpretation is supported at the chromatin-state level, and finally into Task 10, where the result will be visualised along chr21.

Task 7.1: Broad peak calling for histone marks

Histone marks are not all alike. They can have sharp, broad, and mixed signal profiles. Our two marks are histone modifications associated with regulatory regions, and H3K4me1 in particular often produces relatively broad enrichment domains.

We will therefore call peaks using MACS2 with broad-peak settings.

Given the goals and time limits of this practical, we will focus here on peak definition and immediate quality assessment. In a longer workshop with additional histone marks, replicates, cell types, or conditions, one natural extension would be differential peak calling.

Call broad peaks for the H3K27ac sample against the shared Input control.

macs2 callpeak \
  -t 0001_bam/H3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam \
  -c 0001_bam/Input_r1.chr21.bam \
  -f BAM \
  -g 4.67e7 \
  -n H3K27ac_r1_chr21 \
  --broad \
  --broad-cutoff 0.1 \
  --outdir 0004_peaks

Same for H3K4me1:

macs2 callpeak \
  -t 0001_bam/H3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam \
  -c 0001_bam/Input_r1.chr21.bam \
  -f BAM \
  -g 4.67e7 \
  -n H3K4me1_r1_chr21 \
  --broad \
  --broad-cutoff 0.1 \
  --outdir 0004_peaks

In this practical, keep -f BAM: the staged chr21 files are single-end BAM files.

In this practical, keep -g 4.67e7, because peak calling is being performed on chr21-restricted BAM files and we use the size of chr21 as a classroom approximation for the effective genome size.

For the rest of this task, focus mainly on the *.broadPeak files, because those are the peak files that will be carried forward into the downstream steps.

Typical output files include:

  • *.broadPeak
  • *.gappedPeak
  • model or log files

A successful MACS2 run should end with output similar to the excerpt below:

# format = BAM
# effective genome size = 4.67e+07
# Broad region calling is on
# Paired-End mode is off
#2 predicted fragment length is 185 bps
#4 Write broad peak in broadPeak format file... 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak
#4 Write broad peak in bed12/gappedPeak format file... 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.gappedPeak
INFO  ... Done!

In this practical, the most important points are that MACS2 recognises the files as single-end (Paired-End mode is off), uses the chr21 effective genome size that we supplied, successfully infers a fragment length, and writes the expected broadPeak and gappedPeak files. The exact read counts, fragment length, and peak totals may vary slightly with software version or preprocessing, but the overall structure of the log should look like this.

Before answering the questions, inspect the peak files directly. First, look at the first few lines so that you can see what a broadPeak file looks like; then compare how many regions were called for each mark and how wide those regions are on average.

Your output should be similar to the examples shown below, although exact values can differ slightly depending on software version and upstream preprocessing.

Look at the first few called broad peaks

head 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak
head 0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak

Example output from this dataset:

chr21   5065383 5065716 H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peak_1 15      .       3.24873 3.6126  1.57438
chr21   5128275 5128511 H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peak_2 47      .       5.17999 6.98643 4.73634
chr21   5240725 5241143 H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peak_3 63      .       5.62155 8.6902  6.3703

[...]

These rows show that a broadPeak file is still basically a genomic interval table. The first three columns are the chromosome, start, and end coordinates; the fourth column is the peak name assigned by MACS2. The later columns contain a score and enrichment statistics. At this stage, students do not need to memorise every column, but they should recognise that each line represents one called broad peak with both genomic coordinates and a measure of confidence.

Summarise the number and mean width of called broad peaks

for f in 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak 0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak; do
  awk 'BEGIN{n=0;sum=0}
       {w=$3-$2; sum+=w; n++}
       END{
         if(n>0){
           printf "%s\tpeaks=%d\tmean_width=%.1f bp\n", FILENAME, n, sum/n
         } else {
           printf "%s\tpeaks=0\tmean_width=NA\n", FILENAME
         }
       }' "$f"
done

Example output from this dataset:

0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak     peaks=662       mean_width=710.7 bp
0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak     peaks=1607      mean_width=614.1 bp

In this particular run, H3K4me1 produces more called broad peaks on chr21, but H3K27ac has the larger mean peak width. That is a useful reminder that “more peaks” and “broader peaks” are not the same thing. Because this analysis is being run on a chr21 subset with a specific MACS2 broad-peak setting, the exact numbers should not be over-generalised; what matters more is that the two histone marks do not produce identical peak landscapes, which is biologically reasonable for marks with related but distinct regulatory associations (Heintzman 2009; Creyghton 2010; Calo 2013).

Inspect the five broadest called regions for each mark

for f in 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak 0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak; do
  echo "### $f"
  awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {print $1, $2, $3, $3-$2}' "$f" | sort -k4,4nr | sed -n '1,5p'
done

Example output from this dataset:

### 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak
chr21   34906171        34910344        4173
chr21   31734458        31738607        4149
chr21   35025666        35029657        3991
chr21   14451569        14455457        3888
chr21   46320030        46323890        3860

### 0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak
chr21   14450597        14455911        5314
chr21   39315374        39320548        5174
chr21   29639150        29644189        5039
chr21   42543810        42548415        4605
chr21   38850282        38854303        4021

These results are interesting because they show that H3K4me1 contains some of the widest individual peaks in the dataset, even though its mean peak width is smaller than that of H3K27ac. In other words, the extreme tail of the width distribution and the average width can tell slightly different stories. This is exactly why it is worth looking at both a summary statistic and a few concrete examples rather than relying on a single number.

NoteT7 Q1

Using the summary command above, which mark produces more called broad-peak regions on chr21, and how many regions were called for each sample?

NoteT7 Q2

Using the width summary above, which mark has the larger mean peak width in this dataset? Does that agree with the list of the five broadest individual peaks, and what does that tell you about the difference between an average and the extreme tail of a distribution?

NoteT7 Q3

Why is it important to compare each ChIP sample against Input during peak calling, and why should the Input sample still not be assumed to be perfectly flat across the chromosome?

Task 7.2: Peak quality control - percentage of reads in peaks

A good way to test whether the called peaks truly capture a substantial proportion of the ChIP signal is by checking the percentage of reads in peaks. FRiP-style summaries are part of standard ChIP-seq quality assessment practice (Landt 2012).

A simplified FRiP-like summary10 can be computed by combining samtools (Li 2009) and bedtools (Quinlan and Hall 2010): count how many aligned reads overlap the called peaks and divide by the total number of mapped reads.

Build a simplified FRiP-like summary for both histone-mark samples. First create the output file and write its header:

printf "sample\ttotal_reads\treads_in_peaks\tpercent_reads_in_peaks\n" > 0006_results/Task7_FRiP_like_summary.tsv

Count mapped reads, sum reads overlapping peaks, and calculate the FRiP-like percentage.

for mark in H3K27ac H3K4me1; do
  total=$(samtools view -c -F 4 0001_bam/${mark}_r1.chr21.bam)

  bedtools coverage -counts \
    -a 0004_peaks/${mark}_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak \
    -b 0001_bam/${mark}_r1.chr21.bam \
    > 0006_results/${mark}_peak_read_counts.tsv

  inpeaks=$(awk '{sum += $NF} END{print sum+0}' 0006_results/${mark}_peak_read_counts.tsv)
  pct=$(awk -v a="$inpeaks" -v b="$total" 'BEGIN{printf "%.2f", 100*a/b}')

  printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n" "$mark" "$total" "$inpeaks" "$pct" >> 0006_results/Task7_FRiP_like_summary.tsv
done

Display the summary table in a readable format.

column -t 0006_results/Task7_FRiP_like_summary.tsv

Example output from this dataset:

sample   total_reads  reads_in_peaks  percent_reads_in_peaks
H3K27ac  138349       52412           37.88
H3K4me1  123943       50828           41.01

The files H3K27ac_peak_read_counts.tsv and H3K4me1_peak_read_counts.tsv are intermediate tables, not the final percentage by themselves. Each row corresponds to one called peak, and the last column reports how many aligned reads overlap that peak. To obtain the simplified FRiP-like value, sum the last column and divide by the total number of mapped reads for that sample.

In this practical, these values should be interpreted comparatively, not as strict pass/fail thresholds, because they are computed on chr21-restricted files and broad peak sets rather than on full-genome peak calls. The main point is that the two histone marks are not identical: H3K4me1 appears to distribute reads across more peak regions, while H3K27ac appears to concentrate signal in fewer but broader domains. That is broadly compatible with the known biology of these marks, while still remaining a coarse classroom-scale summary (Heintzman 2009; Creyghton 2010; Calo 2013; Landt 2012).

A higher FRiP-like percentage means that a larger fraction of reads falls inside the called peaks, which is usually consistent with stronger enrichment and better signal-to-noise (Landt 2012). In this dataset, both histone-mark samples place a substantial fraction of their chr21 reads inside their own called broad peaks: 37.88% for H3K27ac and 41.01% for H3K4me1. The main practical meaning of this result is that both peak sets look coherent enough to carry forward into downstream interpretation, rather than being obviously too diffuse or too weak to use.

The slightly higher FRiP-like value for H3K4me1 means that, with these MACS2 settings on chr21, a somewhat larger fraction of H3K4me1 reads is captured by its own peak set. That does not by itself mean that H3K4me1 is biologically “stronger” or more important than H3K27ac. FRiP-like summaries are quality-control measures, not direct functional annotations. They should therefore be interpreted together with the browser-style inspection, the peak-count summary, the peak-width summary, and the comparison to Input (Landt 2012).

To examine the Input sample properly, do not call a separate FRiP from an Input peak set. Instead, reuse the already called H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peak regions as the reference intervals, and ask how many Input reads fall inside those same regions. This is the decisive control comparison for Task 7.2, because these are exactly the peak sets that we would like to treat as candidate regulatory regions in Task 8.

Count Input reads inside each histone-mark peak set

printf "peak_set\tinput_total_reads\tinput_reads_in_peaks\tinput_percent_in_peaks\n" > 0006_results/Task7_Input_in_histone_peaks.tsv

input_total=$(samtools view -c -F 4 0001_bam/Input_r1.chr21.bam)

for mark in H3K27ac H3K4me1; do
  bedtools coverage -counts \
    -a 0004_peaks/${mark}_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak \
    -b 0001_bam/Input_r1.chr21.bam \
    > 0006_results/Input_in_${mark}_peaks.tsv

  input_in_peaks=$(awk '{sum += $NF} END{print sum+0}' 0006_results/Input_in_${mark}_peaks.tsv)
  input_pct=$(awk -v a="$input_in_peaks" -v b="$input_total" 'BEGIN{printf "%.2f", 100*a/b}')

  printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n" "$mark" "$input_total" "$input_in_peaks" "$input_pct" >> 0006_results/Task7_Input_in_histone_peaks.tsv
done

column -t 0006_results/Task7_Input_in_histone_peaks.tsv

If the Input sample also shows substantial read accumulation inside the histone-mark peak regions, that suggests that some of the apparent ChIP enrichment may reflect background structure, local accessibility, or other non-specific biases rather than strongly mark-specific signal. If, on the other hand, the Input percentages are clearly lower than the corresponding ChIP percentages, then the peak sets have passed an important quality-control checkpoint and can be carried forward with more confidence into Task 8. The key question here is therefore not “is the number high or low in absolute terms?”, but rather “does the ChIP sample concentrate reads in these regions more strongly than the matched control?” (Landt 2012).

NoteT7 Q4

Which histone mark has the higher simplified FRiP-like percentage on chr21? Based on this result together with the peak-count and peak-width summaries, would you keep both peak sets for downstream interpretation in Task 8, or would you already be concerned about one of them?

NoteT7 Q5

After counting Input reads inside the H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peak regions, do the control percentages look clearly lower than the corresponding ChIP percentages? Based on that comparison, is it justified to carry these peak sets forward into Task 8 as candidate regulatory regions?

Task 8: Enhansemble - intersecting peaks and annotating candidate active regulatory regions

We will now combine both histone marks. Regions enriched for both H3K4me1 and H3K27ac are often interpreted as stronger candidates for active enhancer-like regions than regions marked by only one of them, because H3K4me1 marks enhancer-like elements and H3K27ac is associated with active enhancer activity (Heintzman 2009; Creyghton 2010).

This task has three parts:

  1. intersect the H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peak sets,
  2. compute simple reads-in-peaks summaries,
  3. annotate the overlapping regions to nearby genes.

These overlap-derived regions will then be carried forward into Task 9, where we will binarise the histone ChIP-seq data, learn a small ChromHMM model on chr21, and ask whether the resulting chromatin states support the enhancer-like interpretation suggested by the peak overlap. In Task 10, we will then visualise those same regions together with the learned state segmentation along the chromosome.

Intersect the peak sets:

bedtools intersect \
  -u \
  -a 0004_peaks/H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak \
  -b 0004_peaks/H3K4me1_r1_chr21_peaks.broadPeak \
  > 0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_chr21.bed

We have preinstalled Homer in the workstation for the course. We can use it to annotate the overlapping regions:

annotatePeaks.pl \
  0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_chr21.bed hg38 \
  > 0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_annotated.txt

However, sometimes Homer might not be available. If this is the case, use bedtools closest with the chr21_genes.bed file exported in Task 6, which was already written in bedtools-compatible coordinate order. This fallback gives one row per overlapping peak region together with the nearest annotated gene:

bedtools closest \
  -a 0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_chr21.bed \
  -b 0005_annotation/chr21_genes.bed \
  > 0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_nearest_gene.tsv

Summarise the overlap and inspect the nearest-gene table in R:

overlap <- read.delim(
  "0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_nearest_gene.tsv",
  header = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

nrow(overlap)
head(overlap)

Example output from this dataset:

[1] 599

2 chr21 5242767 5244538  H3K27ac_r1_chr21_peak_5 176  .  8.98242 20.22390 17.69190 chr21 5155498

In this dataset, nrow(overlap) = 599 means that 599 H3K27ac peaks on chr21 also overlap an H3K4me1 peak, so these regions are our first-pass set of candidate active regulatory loci. In the table, columns V1–V9 come from the overlapping H3K27ac broadPeak record, while columns V10–V15 come from the nearest-gene BED record produced by bedtools closest. Because the gene annotation was exported from the UCSC knownGene/TxDb resource, the gene identifier column is a numeric gene ID rather than a gene symbol. It is normal for several nearby overlapping peaks to point to the same nearest gene, as seen in the first rows above. This table is useful because it connects the peak overlap step to a biological interpretation: it lets us move from “regions marked by both histone modifications” to “candidate regulatory regions that may act near specific genes”, which is the basis for the downstream interpretation in Task 9.

NoteT8 Q1

NoteT8 Q2

NoteT8 Q3

This is also a natural bridge to session 10 next week, about functional enrichment analysis with Eszter Ari. If you obtain a set of genes near candidate enhancer-like regions today, the next obvious question is whether they converge on shared biological processes or pathways. Later in the course, session 11 will return to questions of cell-type-specific regulation from a different angle through single-cell transcriptomics. One long-term motivation for epigenomic profiling is precisely to understand the regulatory basis of the expression differences observed across cell types.

Task 9: Stateforge - learning and interpreting chromatin states with ChromHMM

Until here we have followed Chapter 9 of Altuna Akalin’s book, Computational Genomics with R. The chapter ends by emphasising that once we start integrating multiple ChIP-style datasets, pairwise peak comparisons are not always enough. A natural next step is to classify the genome into recurrent combinations of signals. One widely used framework in epigenomics for this is chromatin-state segmentation, often performed with tools such as ChromHMM (Ernst and Kellis 2012).

In large reference-epigenome studies, the algorithm ChromHMM (“Chromatin states using a Hidden Markov Model”) is often run on broader histone panels. For example, the Roadmap Epigenomics project used a core five-mark framework and binarised ChIP-seq signal in 200-bp bins relative to control data before learning chromatin-state models (Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium 2015). Here we will follow the same logic, but in a much simpler adaptation: we will use only H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and the shared Input control on chr21.

This task connects directly to the earlier exercises:

  • Task 6 (Genomaplex) asked whether the signal falls into biologically plausible genomic categories.
  • Task 7 (Peaksmith) identified enriched regions for each histone mark.
  • Task 8 (Enhansemble) defined regions jointly marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me1.
  • Task 9 (Stateforge) now asks whether a learned chromatin-state model agrees with that interpretation.
  • Task 10 (Karyoscape) will then place those regions and states back onto chr21 as a final chromosome-level visualisation.

Because we are using only two marks, the resulting states will be coarser than in large multi-mark studies. That is expected. The important learning goal here is to understand the workflow:

Conceptually, this is not so far from session 8 (Transcriptomics, Part 2): there, we used matrix-based summaries, clustering logic, and interpretation of structured biological patterns to understand transcriptomic variation; here, the matrix is different, but the same habit of interpretation applies.

  1. prepare a cell-mark input table and a chr21 size file,
  2. binarise the aligned ChIP-seq reads against Input,
  3. learn a small model,
  4. inspect the emission matrix,
  5. interpret the peak-overlap regions in the context of the learned states.

9.1 Prepare the ChromHMM input files

Create a tab-separated file called 0007_states/k562_cellmarkfiletable.tsv with one row per histone mark.

printf "K562\tH3K27ac\tH3K27ac_r1.chr21.bam\tInput_r1.chr21.bam\nK562\tH3K4me1\tH3K4me1_r1.chr21.bam\tInput_r1.chr21.bam\n" > 0007_states/k562_cellmarkfiletable.tsv
cat 0007_states/k562_cellmarkfiletable.tsv

The first column is the cell type, the second is the mark, the third is the ChIP BAM filename, and the fourth is the matching control BAM filename. The filenames should match files present in 0001_bam/.

We also need a simple chromosome-size file, 0000_metadata/hg38_chr21.chrom.sizes, for ChromHMM. In this chr21-only practical, create it directly in bash before running ChromHMM:

printf "chr21\t46709983\n" > 0000_metadata/hg38_chr21.chrom.sizes
cat 0000_metadata/hg38_chr21.chrom.sizes

9.2 Binarise the BAM files with ChromHMM

ChromHMM works from binarised mark-presence data. We will binarise the K562 chr21 single-end BAM files in 200-bp bins, using the shared Input control during thresholding.

Now we are ready to run ChromHMM:

java -mx4000M -jar /shared/software/ChromHMM-1.27/ChromHMM/ChromHMM.jar BinarizeBam \
  -b 200 \
  0000_metadata/hg38_chr21.chrom.sizes \
  0001_bam \
  0007_states/k562_cellmarkfiletable.tsv \
  0007_states/binary

If in another project you have paired-end BAM files, you will need to add the -paired flag (but not here, since we know they are single-end).

9.3 Learn a small chromatin-state model

In this context, training a model means asking ChromHMM to look across all 200-bp bins on chr21, detect recurring combinations of H3K27ac and H3K4me1 signal, and group those bins into a small number of hidden chromatin states. During training, the algorithm estimates two things from the data: the emission probabilities, which describe how strongly each state is associated with the two histone marks, and the transition probabilities, which describe how likely one state is to be followed by another along the chromosome. The goal is not to memorise individual bins, but to learn a compact state model that can later be used to segment chr21 and interpret the candidate regulatory regions from Task 8 in a broader chromatin-state context (Ernst and Kellis 2012).

With only two histone marks, a small model is more realistic than the richer 15-state or 18-state models used in broader epigenome projects. For this classroom example, we will learn a 4-state model on chr21. With only H3K27ac and H3K4me1, four states are easier to fit and interpret in a stable way than a larger model on this reduced teaching dataset (Ernst and Kellis 2012). Because this practical is often run from a browser-based or headless server session, we also disable image generation and browser opening in the ChromHMM command below.11

java -Djava.awt.headless=true -mx4000M -jar /shared/software/ChromHMM-1.27/ChromHMM/ChromHMM.jar LearnModel \
  -b 200 \
  -p 0 \
  -noimage \
  -nobrowser \
  0007_states/binary \
  0007_states/model \
  4 \
  hg38

This command should produce files such as:

  • emissions_4.txt
  • transitions_4.txt
  • model_4.txt
  • K562_4_segments.bed
  • K562_4_overlap.txt
  • K562_4_RefSeqTSS_neighborhood.txt
  • K562_4_RefSeqTES_neighborhood.txt

Example output from this dataset:

Using 1 thread for Baum-Welch training
Writing to file 0007_states/model/transitions_4.txt
Writing to file 0007_states/model/emissions_4.txt
Writing to file 0007_states/model/model_4.txt
 Iteration  Estimated Log Likelihood     Change    Total Time (secs)
         1                -26416.845          -                  0.2
         2                -21956.811   4460.033                  0.4
         3                -21217.169    739.643                  0.5
         4                -20704.679    512.489                  0.7
         ...
        91                -19810.874      0.001                  7.4
        92                -19810.873      0.001                  7.4
        93                -19810.872      0.001                  7.5

Warning could not automatically open in a browser 0007_states/model/webpage_4.html

This output shows that the model training ran successfully. The transitions_4.txt, emissions_4.txt, and model_4.txt files store the learned transition probabilities, emission probabilities, and full model parameters, respectively. The iteration table reports the Baum–Welch optimisation: the estimated log-likelihood improves rapidly at first and then changes only slightly, indicating that the model is approaching convergence. The key downstream file for the next step is K562_4_segments.bed, which contains the chromatin-state segmentation along chr21. The final browser-opening warning can be ignored in a server or browser-based session, because it reflects the lack of a local graphical browser rather than a failure of model learning.12

Because the cell name in the cell-mark table is fixed to K562, the segmentation file will be called K562_4_segments.bed.

9.4 Inspect the emission matrix and propose state labels

The most important model-level output is the emission matrix. It tells you, for each state, how strongly that state is associated with H3K27ac and H3K4me1.

emissions <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/model/emissions_4.txt",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

emissions

Look at the states and answer:

  • which states show strong H3K4me1 but weak H3K27ac?
  • which states show strong signal for both marks?
  • which states show little or no signal for either mark?

Then create a file with simple labels for the states, such as H3K27ac_dominant, H3K4me1_dominant, both_high, or both_weak. Save the table as 0007_states/state_labels.tsv using the code below, after replacing the placeholder labels with your own interpretation of the emission matrix:

state_labels <- data.frame(
  state_id = paste0("E", 1:4),
  state_label = c(
    "label1",
    "label2",
    "label3",
    "label4"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

state_labels

write.table(
  state_labels,
  file = "0007_states/state_labels.tsv",
  sep = "\t",
  quote = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

Your final file should look like this structure:

state_id    state_label
E1  label1
E2  label2
E3  label3
E4  label4

The exact labels are up to your interpretation of the emission matrix. Avoid over-interpreting the states as a full promoter/enhancer/repressed catalogue, because that level of chromatin-state annotation usually relies on a broader histone panel (Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium 2015; Ernst and Kellis 2017).

9.5 Intersect the overlap-derived regions with the learned segmentation

Now compare the Task 8 overlap-derived regions to the segmentation learned by ChromHMM, so that each candidate regulatory region can later be assigned to a dominant chromatin state.

Because a single broad overlap-derived region can span several consecutive 200-bp ChromHMM segments, it is more informative to record the number of overlapping base pairs than to treat every intersect row as an equal event.

This file is not the final biological summary by itself; it is the bridge between the candidate regulatory regions from Task 8 and the state-based interpretation that you will construct in Task 9.6.

bedtools intersect \
  -wo \
  -a 0006_results/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_chr21.bed \
  -b 0007_states/model/K562_4_segments.bed \
  > 0007_states/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_vs_ChromHMM.tsv

Inspect the first rows of the intersection table in R:

state_hits <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_vs_ChromHMM.tsv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

colnames(state_hits) <- c(
  "peak_chr", "peak_start", "peak_end", "peak_id", "peak_score",
  "peak_strand", "peak_signal", "peak_pvalue", "peak_qvalue",
  "state_chr", "state_start", "state_end", "state_id", "overlap_bp"
)

head(state_hits)
