6     7.50834     chr21     5246800   5250200       E2         65

This output shows why the intersection table is useful. The first nine columns describe one overlap-derived peak region from Task 8, the next four columns describe one ChromHMM segment, and the last column gives the number of overlapping base pairs. Because one broad peak can span several consecutive ChromHMM segments, the same peak may appear in multiple rows with different state labels and different overlap widths. This is expected, not a problem: it shows that the peak is crossing a local chromatin-state boundary. In the next step, you will use this table to assign each overlap-derived region to the state covering the largest number of overlapping base pairs, so that each candidate regulatory region receives one dominant ChromHMM state for interpretation.

9.6 Summarise the learned state assignments in R

In the table produced above, columns 1–9 come from the Task 8 overlap-derived broadPeak record, columns 10–13 come from the ChromHMM segmentation, and the final column gives the number of overlapping base pairs.

Assign each overlap-derived region to the ChromHMM state with the largest number of overlapping base pairs:

state_hits <- state_hits[order(state_hits$peak_id, -state_hits$overlap_bp), ]

peak_state <- state_hits[!duplicated(state_hits$peak_id), c("peak_id", "state_id", "overlap_bp")]

state_labels <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/state_labels.tsv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

Create the state summary:

state_summary <- as.data.frame(table(peak_state$state_id), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
colnames(state_summary) <- c("state_id", "n_regions")

state_summary <- merge(state_summary, state_labels, by = "state_id", all.x = TRUE)
state_summary$fraction <- state_summary$n_regions / sum(state_summary$n_regions)

state_summary

Save the plot:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(
  state_summary,
  aes(x = reorder(ifelse(is.na(state_label), state_id, state_label), -fraction), y = fraction)
) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw() +
  xlab("Dominant ChromHMM state") +
  ylab("Fraction of overlap-derived regions") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggsave("0007_states/Task9_overlap_state_distribution.png", width = 8, height = 4)

This summary is now based on one dominant ChromHMM state per overlap-derived region, rather than on raw intersect rows. That makes the interpretation cleaner: each candidate regulatory region from Task 8 is assigned to the state that covers the largest part of that region.

In this dataset, the dominant-state summary should look like this:

This is the point where the practical moves from producing files to testing a biological hypothesis.

The graph above is not just a summary of which bar is tallest. It asks whether the candidate regulatory regions from Task 8 remain convincing when viewed through an independent, model-based chromatin-state framework. In this dataset, most overlap-derived regions are assigned to the both_strong state, while smaller fractions fall into H3K27ac_dominant, H3K4me1_dominant, or both_weak states. That is an encouraging result: it means that the majority of regions jointly marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me1 are also placed by ChromHMM into the state with strongest combined signal for both marks.

This strengthens the interpretation developed across the earlier tasks. In Task 7, the peak sets passed basic quality-control checks. In Task 8, overlapping H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peaks were used as a first-pass set of candidate active regulatory loci. Now, in Task 9, the chromatin-state model provides an additional layer of support: most of those candidate loci are assigned to a state compatible with strong signal for both marks, rather than being scattered mainly across weak or ambiguous states.

The smaller secondary classes are still biologically informative. Regions assigned to H3K27ac_dominant may reflect loci with stronger acetylation than methylation, whereas H3K4me1_dominant regions may include weaker or less active enhancer-like loci. The very small both_weak fraction suggests that only a minority of the overlap-derived regions are being assigned to a weak-signal state by the model. In other words, the final result is not simply “nice, one column is higher”: it is that the candidate regions identified from peak overlap are, for the most part, supported by an independent chromatin-state model.

This does not prove that every region is a bona fide active enhancer. The practical still uses only two histone marks on chr21, so the final interpretation should remain cautious. But it does give a biologically meaningful endpoint for Task 9: the workflow has narrowed chr21 down to a set of candidate regulatory regions that are supported by read enrichment, peak overlap, nearest-gene association, and dominant assignment to a both-strong chromatin state. In the next task, we will place these same regions back onto chr21 in a chromosome-level view so that the result can be inspected visually as well as statistically.

NoteT9 Q1

Which files produced by BinarizeBam confirm that the K562 histone ChIP-seq data were successfully converted into ChromHMM binary input?

NoteT9 Q2

Based on emissions_4.txt, which state or states look most compatible with enhancer-like chromatin, and why?

NoteT9 Q3

After assigning each overlap-derived region to the ChromHMM state with the largest base-pair overlap, do the regions fall primarily into the state labelled as both_strong (or otherwise enhancer-like)?

Task 10: Karyoscape - visualising candidate regulatory states along chr21

By the end of Task 9, we have already built and interpreted a small chromatin-state model. The remaining question is how those assignments are arranged along the chromosome. A chromosome-level visualisation helps us see whether the candidate regions form isolated loci, local clusters, or broader domains, and it gives us a satisfying final view of how the peak-overlap regions relate to the learned ChromHMM segmentation.

This task has three parts:

  1. prepare the segmentation and overlap-derived regions for plotting,
  2. customise colours and layout for a chromosome-level figure,
  3. draw and save a final chr21 visualisation with karyoploteR.

We will use the karyoploteR package, which is designed for plotting data along a linear genome. Here we will create a two-track chr21 view:

  • the top track will show the overlap-derived candidate regulatory regions from Task 8, coloured by their dominant ChromHMM state;
  • the bottom track will show the full ChromHMM segmentation across chr21.

This does not replace the summary statistics from Task 9.6; instead, it complements them by adding the genomic context. It also gives you a final figure that you can inspect visually and tweak by changing colours, margins, zoom settings, or optional gene labels.

We start by loading the libraries:

library(karyoploteR)
library(GenomicRanges)

Load the ChromHMM segments and attach the chosen state labels.

state_labels <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/state_labels.tsv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

segments <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/model/K562_4_segments.bed",
  header = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
colnames(segments) <- c("chr", "start", "end", "state_id")

segments <- merge(segments, state_labels, by = "state_id", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
segments$state_label[is.na(segments$state_label)] <- segments$state_id

Read the peak–state intersections and sort them by overlap size.

overlap_hits <- read.delim(
  "0007_states/H3K27ac_H3K4me1_overlap_vs_ChromHMM.tsv",
  header = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
colnames(overlap_hits) <- c(
  "peak_chr", "peak_start", "peak_end", "peak_id", "peak_score",
  "peak_strand", "peak_signal", "peak_pvalue", "peak_qvalue",
  "state_chr", "state_start", "state_end", "state_id", "overlap_bp"
)

overlap_hits <- overlap_hits[order(overlap_hits$peak_id, -overlap_hits$overlap_bp), ]

Assign one dominant state per region and define plotting colours.

peak_state <- overlap_hits[!duplicated(overlap_hits$peak_id),
                           c("peak_chr", "peak_start", "peak_end", "peak_id", "state_id", "overlap_bp")]

peak_state <- merge(peak_state, state_labels, by = "state_id", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
peak_state$state_label[is.na(peak_state$state_label)] <- peak_state$state_id

# Edit these colours if you want to try a different palette
state_cols <- c(
  both_strong = "#D73027",
  H3K27ac_dominant = "#FC8D59",
  H3K4me1_dominant = "#4575B4",
  both_weak = "#BDBDBD"
)

legend_labels <- c(
  "both strong",
  "H3K27ac dom.",
  "H3K4me1 dom.",
  "both weak"
)

segment_cols <- state_cols[segments$state_label]
segment_cols[is.na(segment_cols)] <- "#BDBDBD"
segment_cols <- adjustcolor(segment_cols, alpha.f = 0.45)
segment_cols[segments$state_label == "both_weak"] <- "#E6E6E6"

peak_cols <- adjustcolor(state_cols[peak_state$state_label], alpha.f = 0.90)
peak_cols[is.na(peak_cols)] <- adjustcolor("#969696", alpha.f = 0.90)

# For the top track, use the midpoint of each overlap-derived region so the
# markers remain visible at chromosome scale.
peak_mid <- floor((peak_state$peak_start + peak_state$peak_end) / 2)

Tune margins and panel sizes for the chromosome plot, and add placeholder for gene labels:

plot.params <- getDefaultPlotParams(plot.type = 2)
plot.params$leftmargin <- 0.10
plot.params$rightmargin <- 0.20
plot.params$topmargin <- 35
plot.params$bottommargin <- 28
plot.params$data1height <- 85
plot.params$data2height <- 125
plot.params$ideogramheight <- 18

gene_gr <- GRanges()

Optional zoom: edit and use this code if you want to inspect a smaller part of chr21

zoom_region <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(34000000, 37000000))

Optional gene labels: edit and use this code if you want to highlight one or more loci on chr21

gene_gr <- GRanges(
  seqnames = c("chr21"),
  ranges = IRanges(
    start = c(34787801),
    end = c(36004667)
  )
)

mcols(gene_gr)$gene <- c("RUNX1")

Draw the chr21 plot, add the two tracks, and save the image.

png("0007_states/Task10_karyoploteR_chr21_states.png", width = 2100, height = 900, res = 180)

kp <- plotKaryotype(
  genome = "hg38",
  chromosomes = "chr21",
  plot.type = 2,
  plot.params = plot.params
  # zoom = zoom_region
)

kpDataBackground(kp, data.panel = 1, color = "#FAFAFA")
kpDataBackground(kp, data.panel = 2, color = "#FAFAFA")
kpAddBaseNumbers(kp, tick.dist = 5000000, add.units = TRUE, cex = 0.8)

# Top panel: plot overlap-derived regions as thicker vertical markers so they
# remain visible at whole-chromosome scale.
kpSegments(
  kp,
  chr = peak_state$peak_chr,
  x0 = peak_mid,
  x1 = peak_mid,
  y0 = 0.18,
  y1 = 0.82,
  col = peak_cols,
  lwd = 2.2,
  data.panel = 1
)

# Bottom panel: full ChromHMM segmentation along chr21
# For visualisation only, enforce a minimum display width for non-both_weak states
# so they remain visible at whole-chromosome scale.
chr21_length <- 46709983L
min_state_width_bp <- 100000L

segment_plot_start <- segments$start + 1L
segment_plot_end <- segments$end
segment_mid <- floor((segment_plot_start + segment_plot_end) / 2)

is_nonweak <- segments$state_label != "both_weak"
segment_width <- segment_plot_end - segment_plot_start + 1L
needs_widening <- is_nonweak & segment_width < min_state_width_bp

segment_plot_start[needs_widening] <- pmax(
  1L,
  segment_mid[needs_widening] - floor(min_state_width_bp / 2)
)
segment_plot_end[needs_widening] <- pmin(
  chr21_length,
  segment_mid[needs_widening] + ceiling(min_state_width_bp / 2) - 1L
)

kpRect(
  kp,
  chr = segments$chr,
  x0 = segment_plot_start,
  x1 = segment_plot_end,
  y0 = 0.28,
  y1 = 0.82,
  col = segment_cols,
  border = NA,
  data.panel = 2
)

# Optional: highlight and label selected genes
if (length(gene_gr) > 0) {
  gene_mid <- start(gene_gr) + floor((end(gene_gr) - start(gene_gr)) / 2)

  # Light highlight of the gene span on the ChromHMM panel
  kpRect(
    kp,
    chr = as.character(seqnames(gene_gr)),
    x0 = start(gene_gr),
    x1 = end(gene_gr),
    y0 = 0.12,
    y1 = 0.25,
    col = adjustcolor("#800080", alpha.f = 0.5),
    lwd = 0.8,
    data.panel = 2
  )

  kpText(
    kp,
    chr = as.character(seqnames(gene_gr)),
    x = gene_mid,
    y = 0.17,
    labels = mcols(gene_gr)$gene,
    pos = 3,
    data.panel = 2
  )
}

par(xpd = NA)
usr <- par("usr")

legend(
  x = usr[2] - 0.18 * (usr[2] - usr[1]),
  y = usr[4] + 0.10 * (usr[4] - usr[3]),
  legend = legend_labels,
  fill = unname(state_cols),
  border = NA,
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.9,
  title = "State",
  xjust = 0,
  yjust = 1
)

mtext(
  "Top: overlap-derived regions from Task 8",
  side = 3,
  line = 1.0,
  adj = 0.18,
  cex = 0.95
)

mtext(
  "Bottom: ChromHMM segmentation on chr21",
  side = 1,
  line = 1.8,
  adj = 0.18,
  cex = 0.95
)

dev.off()

This code reads the segmentation and overlap files created in the previous steps, assigns one dominant state per overlap-derived region, and then plots both layers along the same chromosome. The top panel answers “where are the candidate regions we carried forward from Task 8?”, while the bottom panel shows the underlying ChromHMM state structure across the whole of chr21. After you get the first version working, try changing the colour palette, margins, zoom settings, or optional GRanges gene labels to make the chromosome view clearer and more biologically informative. To add more genes, extend the seqnames, start, end, and gene vectors with one extra entry per gene.13

The resulting figure should look like this:

Suggested interpretation workflow

If you finish the tasks, try to summarise the whole analysis in the following order:

  1. Metadata and design: which experiments and controls did we analyse?
  2. Global quality: do the samples cluster as expected?
  3. Local inspection: do the browser tracks show convincing enrichment above Input?
  4. Technical bias: are the GC-bias patterns or cross-correlation profiles suspicious?
  5. Biological plausibility: do the marks concentrate in plausible regulatory categories?
  6. Peak-level interpretation: do the called regions and reads-in-peaks summaries support successful enrichment?
  7. Peak-overlap interpretation: which regions jointly marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me1 look most like candidate active regulatory loci?
  8. Chromatin-state interpretation: do the ChromHMM state labels support an enhancer-like / both-high interpretation of those regions, or do they instead suggest more H3K4me1-dominant, H3K27ac-dominant, mixed, or weak-signal states?

What we are not doing today

To keep the practical focused and feasible, we are not including the following as core tasks:

  • FastQC on raw reads
  • read mapping with Bowtie2 or a similar aligner
  • differential peak calling between conditions
  • motif discovery as a main endpoint
  • training a large multi-mark genome-wide ChromHMM model

This practical starts from already prepared BAM and bigWig files, so the focus is on interpretation, quality assessment, peak calling, overlap analysis, chromatin-state modelling, and chromosome-level visualisation rather than on raw-read preprocessing.

We do, however, include a hands-on ChromHMM step on a reduced two-mark chr21 example, because it gives you direct experience with binarisation, model learning, and state interpretation in a manageable classroom setting.

NoteBonus Q3

Footnotes

  1. Restricting the analysis to chr21 is a pedagogical shortcut to keep runtime manageable in class, since chr21 is the smallest human autosome. For real histone ChIP-seq studies, quality control, peak calling, and downstream interpretation should normally be assessed genome-wide.↩︎

  2. We use the BAM file with Output = alignments rather than unfiltered alignments because alignments is the filtered, analysis-ready version of the mapped reads. Using the filtered BAM makes the downstream practical more reproducible and avoids giving different students files that still contain reads usually removed before analysis.↩︎

  3. We use the bigWig file with Output = fold change over control rather than signal p-value because in this practical the bigWig files are mainly used as genome-browser tracks. Fold change over control is easier to interpret visually as enrichment over the matched input, whereas signal p-value reflects statistical confidence rather than signal magnitude. The input sample is left without a bigWig entry in the manifest on purpose, so that all students use the same two histone browser tracks and inspect the input directly from its BAM file.↩︎

  4. If downloading and subsetting the original files becomes too slow or cumbersome during the practical, you can copy the prepared backup files from the shared course folder instead:

    # copy prepared chr21-restricted BAM files
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | cut -f1 | while read s; do
  cp -n "/shared/OMICS/practical_09/0001_bam/${s}.chr21.bam" 0001_bam/
done
    # copy the selected histone bigWig files listed in the manifest
tail -n +2 0000_metadata/encode_k562_manifest.tsv | cut -f10 | grep -v '^$' | while read f; do
  cp -n "/shared/OMICS/practical_09/0002_bigwig/${f}" 0002_bigwig/
done
    ↩︎

  5. RUNX1 has GRCh38 coordinates chr21:34,787,801-36,004,667 and is annotated on the reverse strand. A practical reference to plot the region where the gene starts is chr21:36,004,667, so a convenient 10 kb viewing window is chr21:35,990,000–36,020,000.↩︎

  6. There is no formal minimum number of fragments for a chromosome-restricted file like the chr21 subset used here. Still, chr21 makes up about 1.5% of the GRCh38 genome, so as a rough guide, the 10–20 million whole-genome recommended fragments (ENCODE Data Coordination Center 2020) would scale to about 150,000–300,000 fragments on chr21. In that sense, the 138,349 fragments used here are slightly below the lower end of that rough range, but it’s still valid, since ChIP-seq signal is not uniformly distributed across the genome.↩︎

  7. The horizontal rows in the plot are expected. They arise because each 1-kb bin contains an integer number of mapped fragments, which we can call k = 0, 1, 2, 3, .... These raw counts are not plotted directly. Instead, they are first converted to CPM (counts per million), and only then transformed as log10(CPM + 1).

    For a given sample, the CPM of a bin is calculated as:

    CPM = (raw count in the bin / total counts in the sample) × 10^6

    So the y-axis is really:

    log10(CPM + 1) = log10((k / N) × 10^6 + 1)

    where N is the total number of counted fragments in that sample.

    For example, if the sample has about 124,000 total counts, then:

    • k = 0 gives CPM = 0, so log10(0 + 1) = 0
    • k = 1 gives about 8.1 CPM, so log10(9.1) ≈ 0.96
    • k = 2 gives about 16.1 CPM, so log10(17.1) ≈ 1.23
    • k = 3 gives about 24.2 CPM, so log10(25.2) ≈ 1.40

    This is why the first non-zero row appears much higher than 0.301: the plot uses log10(CPM + 1), not log10(raw count + 1). In other words, the visible horizontal bands correspond to bins with the same raw integer count, after library-size normalisation.↩︎

  8. This task builds the annotation locally with Bioconductor instead of relying on pre-made shared BED files. Students who do not have access to /shared/OMICS can still reproduce it from the package documentation and export their own BED files. Useful links: TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/annotation/html/TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene.html; GenomicFeatures vignette https://bioconductor.posit.co/packages/3.23/bioc/vignettes/GenomicFeatures/inst/doc/GenomicFeatures.html; rtracklayer export documentation https://rdrr.io/bioc/rtracklayer/man/export.html; AnnotationHub how-to pages https://bioconductor.posit.co/packages/3.23/bioc/vignettes/AnnotationHub/inst/doc/AnnotationHub-HOWTO.html.↩︎

  9. The original MACS paper describes the method family behind later MACS2 releases, and it remains the standard citation for this peak-calling framework.↩︎

  10. FRiP stands for fraction of reads in peaks. In production analyses, it is usually computed after consistent filtering choices and on complete peak sets; here we use a simplified classroom approximation based on the staged files (Landt 2012).↩︎

  11. The Java flag -Djava.awt.headless=true tells Java to run without trying to connect to a graphical display server. This is useful on remote servers or browser-based sessions, where ChromHMM can otherwise fail while attempting to create graphics or open browser output. The ChromHMM manual documents -noimage and -nobrowser as options to suppress image and browser-related output, and the maintainer’s issue tracker explicitly notes -Djava.awt.headless=true as a practical workaround for headless environments (Ernst and Kellis 2012; ChromHMM manual; ChromHMM GitHub issue #1).↩︎
